summary: Zhubei — 竹北 — means north of the bamboo. A rapidly growing city near the Hsinchu Science Park, where tech engineers outnumber the famous rice paddies that once defined this land.
Xinyi — 信義 — means faith and righteousness. Home to Taipei 101 and the city's glitziest shopping district. Just 30 years ago, this was all military housing and vegetable farms.
Anping — 安平 — means peaceful. Taiwan's oldest district where Dutch traders built Fort Zeelandia in 1624. Don't leave without trying the famous shrimp crackers from century-old shops.
Shoufeng — 壽豐 — means longevity and abundance. A scenic township cradled between mountains and sea, famous for Liyu Lake where locals say the carp grow as big as dolphins.
Hengchun — 恆春 — means eternal spring, and the weather agrees year-round. Gateway to Kenting beaches, this old walled town still has four original gates from 1879.
Beitou — 北投 — derives from the indigenous Ketagalan word for witch. Famous for hot springs since Japanese colonial times, the sulfurous steam still rises like magic from the valley.
Puli — 埔里 — means flat village in the hills. Nestled in Taiwan's geographic center, its pure spring water makes the island's finest rice wine and crafts perfect paper for calligraphy.
Jiaoxi — 礁溪 — means rocky stream. A hot spring paradise where you can soak your feet for free right on the main street. The water here is carbonate-rich and legendarily good for skin.
Luye — 鹿野 — means deer field, named for the deer that once roamed freely here. Now famous for the annual hot air balloon festival that fills the valley with color each summer.
Lukang — 鹿港 — means deer harbor, once Taiwan's second-largest city. Walk the narrow Nine Turns Lane built to confuse pirates, and taste ox-tongue pastries unchanged for generations.
Sanyi — 三義 — means three righteousnesses. Taiwan's wood carving capital, where master craftsmen transform camphor logs into art. The old mountain railway here inspired countless romantic films.
Alishan — 阿里山 — takes its name from the Tsou indigenous chief Ari. Ride the century-old forest railway to catch the legendary sea of clouds at sunrise. The sacred trees here are over 2,000 years old.
Datong — 大同 — means great harmony. Home to the historic Dadaocheng trading district where tea merchants made fortunes in the 1800s. Dihua Street still sells dried goods from overflowing barrels.
Qijin — 旗津 — means flag crossing, from the banner-shaped sandbar it sits on. Take the ferry for fresh seafood and black sand beaches. The lighthouse here has guided ships since 1883.
Ruifang — 瑞芳 — means auspicious fragrance. Home to Jiufen's lantern-lit alleyways that inspired Spirited Away. The gold mines here once made Taiwan the envy of Asia.
Fengyuan — 豐原 — means abundant plains. The undisputed capital of Taiwanese pastries, where sun cakes were perfected. Locals still argue over which century-old bakery makes them best.
Magong — 馬公 — honors the sea goddess Mazu whose temple anchors this island capital. Basalt columns, pristine beaches, and the freshest seafood await in Taiwan's Mediterranean.
Jincheng — 金城 — means golden fortress. Just miles from mainland China, this former battlefield now charms with traditional villages, kaoliang sorghum liquor, and knife-made from old artillery shells.
Hualien — 花蓮 — means lotus flower. Gateway to Taroko Gorge's marble cliffs, this laid-back city sits where Pacific waves meet towering mountains. The mochi here melts in your mouth.
Daxi — 大溪 — means big stream. A charming old town famous for dried tofu so beloved that people drive hours for it. The baroque-style shophouses date from the prosperous camphor trade era.
Beigang — 北港 — means northern harbor. Home to Taiwan's most important Mazu temple, where the goddess's birthday draws millions of pilgrims. The sesame oil pressed here is Taiwan's finest.
Keelung — 基隆 — means prosperous foundation. Taiwan's rainy harbor city where the night market never sleeps and the seafood rivals anywhere in Asia. Ghost Month festivities here are legendary.
Yanshui — 鹽水 — means salt water, from the brackish lagoon nearby. Each Lantern Festival, brave souls dodge millions of bottle rockets in the world's most dangerous fireworks display.
Yuchi — 魚池 — means fish pond, but it's home to Sun Moon Lake, Taiwan's largest body of water. The Thao indigenous people have lived on these shores for centuries, calling it home.
Donggang — 東港 — means eastern harbor. Taiwan's bluefin tuna capital where the first catch of the season fetches millions. Every three years, a spectacular boat-burning festival honors the plague god.
Wuqi — 梧棲 — means where the phoenix tree rests. A humble fishing port transformed by Taiwan's busiest commercial harbor. The fish market at dawn is pure theater.
Toucheng — 頭城 — means head city, as the first Han settlement in Yilan. Surfers flock to Waiao Beach, and Turtle Island offshore looks exactly like its name suggests.
Hsinchu — 新竹 — means new bamboo. The Windy City of Taiwan, where powerful gusts once dried rice vermicelli and now cool the island's semiconductor empire. Glass art here is world-renowned.
Taitung — 臺東 — means eastern Taiwan. A slow-paced paradise where indigenous cultures thrive and the stars shine brightest. The coastline here feels like the edge of the world.
Chiayi — 嘉義 — means praise righteousness. Gateway to Alishan and birthplace of turkey rice, a humble dish that locals swear can cure any ailment. The old prison is now an oddly charming museum.
Shilin — 士林 — means scholarly forest. Home to the legendary night market where grilled sausages sizzle past midnight. The National Palace Museum holds treasures that once belonged to emperors.
Zuoying — 左營 — means left camp, from Qing dynasty military days. Lotus Pond's dragon and tiger pagodas are iconic, and the old walled village still hums with temples and incense.
Nangan — 南竿 — means southern pole. Matsu's main island where Fujian stone houses cling to hillsides and blue tears bioluminescence lights the summer shores. Time moves differently here.
Tamsui — 淡水 — means fresh water. A romantic riverside town where couples watch sunsets over the strait. Spanish and Dutch forts still stand guard, and agei fried tofu is the must-try snack.
Dajia — 大甲 — means great river turtle. Each spring, millions follow the Mazu pilgrimage from here to Beigang, the world's largest religious procession. Taro pastries here are unforgettable.
Pingxi — 平溪 — means peaceful stream. Famous for sky lanterns that carry wishes heavenward, this former mining town now glows with thousands of floating lights during Lantern Festival.

Nanzhuang — 南庄 — means southern village. A dreamy Hakka hamlet where osmanthus flowers perfume the air and the old street serves sweet potato treats. The Saisiyat tribe's Pasta'ai festival is hauntingly beautiful.
Ludao — 綠島 — means green island, a tropical gem 33km offshore. Snorkel with sea turtles, soak in saltwater hot springs at midnight, and remember this was once Taiwan's most notorious prison.
Lanyu — 蘭嶼 — means orchid island. Home to the Tao people who carve stunning boats and live in semi-underground homes. Flying fish season transforms the island into a living documentary.
Meinong — 美濃 — means beautiful and thick. A proud Hakka stronghold famous for oil-paper umbrellas painted by hand and ban tiao noodles cooked in pork broth. Tobacco barns dot the countryside.

Wanhua — 萬華 — means ten thousand glories. Taipei's oldest neighborhood where Longshan Temple has anchored the community since 1738. Herb Lane still prescribes traditional remedies for modern ailments.
Jiji — 集集 — means gathering place. Rebuilt beautifully after the devastating 1999 earthquake, this little train town charms with its green tunnel of camphor trees and nostalgic wooden station.
Sandimen — 三地門 — means three gates. Gateway to Paiwan indigenous culture where slate stone houses guard mountain villages. The glass bead artistry here tells stories only elders fully understand.
Fengbin — 豐濱 — means abundant shore. Amis tribal country where the Pacific crashes against dramatic cliffs. The Stone Steps fishing tradition remains unchanged for generations.
Fuxing — 復興 — means revival. A mountain Atayal district where cherry blossoms paint the hillsides pink each spring. The Lalashan peaches grown here are the island's sweetest.
Changhua — 彰化 — means manifest transformation. The giant Buddha on Bagua Mountain watches over Taiwan's rice basket. The meatball soup here is legendary, each shop guarding secret recipes.

Wulai — 烏來 — comes from Atayal meaning hot and poisonous, for the steaming springs. Just an hour from Taipei, waterfalls plunge and mochi sizzles on old street grills. Cherry blossoms bloom early here.
Guanziling — 關子嶺 — means pass mountain ridge. Taiwan's only mud hot springs turn your skin silky smooth. The Fire and Water Spring mysteriously burns even as water flows—no one fully explains why.
